intro.title: Fairness in Credit Scoring
intro.lede: How should banks decide who gets a loan?
intro.p1: A bank wants to lend only to people who are likely to repay. Every loan is therefore also a decision about profit and loss.
intro.p2: A credit score estimates how reliably a person repays. A decision threshold sets the score from which a loan is approved.
intro.p3: The dataset contains 400 fictional people from two groups: Pinkville and Greenfield. Each group has 100 creditworthy and 100 non-creditworthy people. Yet the scores are distributed differently in the two groups.
intro.p4: You take the role of a fairness advisor: first look at the two groups, then decide where the decision thresholds should be.
intro.note: All people and places are fictional. The data are for illustration only.
intro.profitText: The bank earns €300 for every repaid loan and loses €700 for every loan that is not repaid.
intro.scoreText: Score ≥ threshold: the person gets a loan. Score < threshold: they do not.
intro.dataText: 400 people from two groups. Each group has 100 creditworthy and 100 non-creditworthy people.

twoPopulations.title: Two Population Groups
twoPopulations.subtitle: What is in the data?
twoPopulations.intro1: The dataset contains 400 people: 200 from Pinkville and 200 from Greenfield.
twoPopulations.intro2: Each group has 100 creditworthy and 100 non-creditworthy people. The starting point is therefore the same.
twoPopulations.intro3: The scores, however, differ: people from Pinkville have higher scores on average than people from Greenfield.
twoPopulations.intro4: This raises the fairness question: what does it mean when a model evaluates two groups differently even though creditworthiness is equally distributed?
twoPopulations.scoreHint: The score ranges from 0 to 100. The higher the score, the more likely the person is to repay the loan.
twoPopulations.taskA: Describe the differences between the two distributions. How can you tell them apart?
twoPopulations.taskB: Why might a single decision threshold be unfair? What should a fair decision take into account?

fairThresholds.title: Fair Decision Thresholds!?
fairThresholds.lede: You are a fairness advisor. Set the rules for granting credit.
fairThresholds.intro: The two charts show the scores of the two groups separately. Use the sliders to set the score from which a loan is approved. You can choose different thresholds for the two groups — or a single shared threshold.
fairThresholds.ruleText: If a person's score is at or above the threshold, they get a loan. If it is below, they do not.
fairThresholds.measuresIntro: The confusion matrix counts how many decisions are correct and incorrect. Four metrics are calculated from it:
fairThresholds.confusionHint: In the confusion matrix, the rows are the actual data and the columns are the model's prediction.
fairThresholds.strategyQuestion: How should Greenfield's threshold be set?
fairThresholds.strategyHint: The three “Same …” strategies set Greenfield’s threshold automatically. With “Independent”, you can set it yourself.
fairThresholds.approximateHint: Scores are discrete. “Same positive rates” and “same true positive rates” can therefore often only be approximated.
fairThresholds.task1: Try the four strategies. Describe what changes for the two groups.
fairThresholds.task2: Which thresholds do you choose? Write down both values and explain your choice.
fairThresholds.task3a: Which metrics mattered most in your choice? Why?
fairThresholds.task3b: Is your choice fair? If yes, why? If not, what would be a fair choice?
fairThresholds.task3c: What is the most important argument for your choice?

about.title: About This Learning Activity
about.articleDescription: This learning activity is based on the following peer-reviewed article, published in Teaching Statistics:
about.articleCitation: Schönbrodt, S., Schneider, S., Podworny, S., & Camminady, T. (2026). A learning activity on fairness in data-driven algorithmic decision-making systems. Teaching Statistics, 48, 33–44.
about.goalText: This short version focuses on two questions: how do the scores of the two groups differ, and which decision thresholds are defensible from a fairness perspective?
about.shortVersionNote: This website is the short version of the full learning activity. It contains the two interactive chapters on population groups and fair decision thresholds.

about.privacyText:
This site does not use cookies or tracking. No data is transmitted to a server.

Only the selected language (fairness.lang) and your notes (fairness.notes.*) are stored locally in your browser. This data does not leave your device. You can remove your notes at any time with “Clear notes”; the language choice remains until you clear your browser data.

The site does not load external fonts or analytics tools.

measures.defAccuracy: Accuracy: Share of correct predictions out of all people.
measures.defPositiveRate: Positive rate: Share of people predicted to repay (prediction: repays) out of all people.
measures.defTruePositiveRate: True positive rate: Share of creditworthy people who actually receive a loan.
measures.defProfit: Profit: €300 for every correctly predicted repayment minus €700 for every incorrectly predicted repayment.
